name: Priya Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out in the flat farm country, a crew of six covering about three hundred square kilometres of fields and long straight roads. We start at the depot at seven, have a coffee, get the job sheet, and drive. Most days it's replacing rotten poles, restringing a span after a combine harvester clipped it, or swapping out the old fuses on the farm transformers. I'm the junior, so I'm digging, rigging, flagging traffic, holding the tag line, and learning to climb properly with my legs shaking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it at your age, and what's the hard part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad was a lineman for thirty years, so I grew up with the trucks. I did hairdressing for twenty years, then the salon closed and I thought, well, Dad always said I'd be good at it. The hard part is the strength and the speed, the young ones are so quick, and the paperwork, which I'm slow at. And the pay, I make less than I did cutting hair on a good week, with a mortgage and two kids and Sam's wages from the tyre shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, all that fuss. At the depot we'd have a laugh about it, someone would say the robots still can't dig a hole in frozen ground. I don't really go online except to look at the school's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things stay as they are, which suits me. I've only just found my feet in this job. I'd like to stay in it until I retire, if they'll have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep turning up, keep learning, try to pass my climbing assessments in the spring. Maybe try to put a bit by from the overtime, but that's been the plan for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Nothing to feel, really, it's just Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any of these AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My daughter showed me one, she asked it to write a poem about our dog, and it was clever enough. I don't see what I'd need it for. I've got a phone for calls and the weather, that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest pressure on your family, if not this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, plain and simple. We've got maybe two weeks of bills in the bank. If the car goes or Sam's hours drop, we're borrowing from his mum again, and I hate that.

S0.say: She'd say all that fuss came to nothing, and the crew would joke that robots still can't dig a hole in frozen ground. She rarely goes online.
S0.think: Things stay as they are, which suits me. I've only just found my feet and I'd like to stay in this job until I retire.
S0.do: Keeps turning up and working toward her climbing assessments in the spring. Hopes, as always, to put a bit of overtime aside.
S0.feel: Fine, nothing much to feel, just an ordinary day.
S0.quote: Someone would say the robots still can't dig a hole in frozen ground.
S0.fieldNote: Priya has no interest in AI tools and has only just found her footing after twenty years cutting hair. Her pressure is money: about two weeks of bills saved and a reluctance to borrow from her mother-in-law again. A plateau suits her just fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see, these things always take longer than they say. At work I'd keep my head down. I'm not one for big opinions about it, the company will do what it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. I'm the newest and the slowest, so if they need fewer people, I can count. But I don't want to start panicking over something that might not touch us out here for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down and try to be as useful as I can, show up early, never say no to a callout. I'd cut back on the little things, the takeaway on Fridays, Ben's extra karate, so we've got a bit more slack. I wouldn't go chasing courses on computers, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear a noise in the house at night and tell yourself it's the cat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your job would you guess go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning, probably, and the checking of the lines, they already fly drones over the big ones. The digging, maybe, if they get a machine that can do it. The climbing and the actual work at the top, I think that's people for a good while yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they started letting people go, or if they stopped taking on apprentices. Or if my foreman, Gary, told me straight to start looking. He's honest, he'd tell me.

S1.say: She'd say these things always take longer than promised and keep her head down at work. She'd leave the big opinions to others, figuring the company will do what it does.
S1.think: I'm the newest and slowest, so if they need fewer people, I can count. But I don't want to panic about something that may not reach us out here for years.
S1.do: Shows up early and never turns down a callout to be as useful as possible. Cuts Friday takeaways and her son's extra karate for slack. Avoids computer courses and waits for a clear sign, such as cuts or her foreman telling her to look.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a noise at night and telling herself it's the cat.
S1.quote: Like when you hear a noise in the house at night and tell yourself it's the cat.
S1.fieldNote: Priya's response to gradual change is to work harder and wait for a clear signal, which she ties to her foreman's honesty. She privately knows she's most exposed as the newest and slowest. She rules out tech courses as not her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody saw this coming and nobody's ready, so everyone's in the same boat. I'd say it to Sam and my mum, not online. At work, I suppose we'd all be saying the same thing, what now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be the first out. I'm not good enough yet to be someone they'd fight to keep. And Sam's job, fixing tyres, I don't know, maybe robots do that too. Two weeks of money and two jobs gone, that's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit down with Sam the first night and work out what we can live on. Cut everything that isn't food, mortgage, power and petrol. I'd go to his parents and ask if we could move in with them if it came to that, they've got the farmhouse with spare rooms. And I'd look at cutting hair again, from the kitchen, because people will still want a person to do their hair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the floor's gone. I'd try not to show the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ellie and Ben?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we'd be okay, Dad and I would sort it out, and they don't need to worry. Ellie's eleven, she'd know I was lying a bit. Ben would ask if he can still have his birthday party, and I'd say yes, whatever it costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about hairdressing again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would. I never thought I'd go back, I was tired of it. But a robot cutting hair? I don't know anyone who'd sit for that. It'd be cash in hand from the kitchen, and that'd keep the lights on.

S2.say: She'd say nobody saw it coming and everyone is in the same boat, but she'd say it to her partner and her mother, not online.
S2.think: I'd be the first out, not good enough yet to be worth fighting for. With two weeks of money and possibly Sam's tyre job gone too, that's frightening.
S2.do: Works out with Sam on the first night what they can live on and cuts everything but food, mortgage, power and petrol. Asks Sam's parents about moving into their farmhouse if needed and goes back to cutting hair from the kitchen for cash.
S2.feel: Sick, as if the floor has gone, while trying to hide it from the kids.
S2.quote: A robot cutting hair? I don't know anyone who'd sit for that.
S2.fieldNote: Priya falls back on what she knows: family and her old trade. She'd cut hair from her kitchen and move in with her in-laws if she had to, but she wouldn't touch new technology. She shows no anger at anyone in particular; it's a shared misfortune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a long time, a lot can happen. To friends I'd probably say let's see what the government does. I'm not one to go on about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I'd lose the job at forty-eight instead of forty-five. I'd be better at it by then, but better at something nobody needs. I'm not going to become a robot expert, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save what I can, even fifty a month, and stop the extras. Keep my hand in with hairdressing, a few clients on Saturdays, so it's there if I need it. And keep working as hard as I can at the lines until they tell me otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried in my stomach, all the time. Five years of waiting for the shoe to drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes when, not what. And maybe it gives Sam time to find something. But it doesn't make me a different person, I'm not going to start loving computers at forty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not one for courses. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I struggled with the theory for my certificate, and that was about electricity, which I understand. I'd rather spend those years getting the most out of the job I have.

S3.say: She'd say five years is a long time and a lot can happen, and that she'd wait to see what the government does.
S3.think: I'd lose the job at 48 instead of 45, better at something nobody needs. I'm not going to become a robot expert.
S3.do: Saves what she can, even 50 a month, and stops the extras. Keeps a few Saturday hairdressing clients as a fallback and works as hard as she can on the lines until told otherwise.
S3.feel: A constant worry in her stomach, five years of waiting for the shoe to drop.
S3.quote: I'd be better at it by then, but better at something nobody needs.
S3.fieldNote: Five years delays Priya's loss but doesn't change her plan, because she won't retrain. She would quietly build up hairdressing as a fallback. The waiting itself becomes a source of stress for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, that's a long way off, we'll cross that bridge. I'd probably say the same at the pub as I'd say at work, which is not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get some good years out of this job, which matters to me, because it's Dad's trade. The kids would be nearly grown. But at fifty-three I'm not starting again, I'd be cutting hair and hoping it's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working the lines, keep a few hair clients, and try to pay a bit more off the mortgage each year. I'd push Ellie and Ben to think about jobs that need people. And maybe ask Gary about getting my ticket faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but slower. It's not a fire, it's a leak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years puts you at fifty-three. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty-three isn't old, but it's too old to start something that needs computers. I'd want the job to see me to sixty. I'd rather it went quietly with me than took me early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want your kids to steer away from line work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to do something with people. Ellie's good at science, maybe she'd be a nurse or a vet. I'd be sad if the trucks stopped going down our road, but I wouldn't want them trapped in it.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a long way off and they'd cross that bridge when they came to it, saying the same little at the pub as at work.
S4.think: I'd get some good years out of Dad's trade and the kids would be nearly grown, but at 53 I'm not starting again; I'd be cutting hair and hoping it's enough.
S4.do: Keeps working the lines, keeps a few hairdressing clients and tries to pay a bit more off the mortgage each year. Pushes her kids toward jobs that need people and asks her foreman about getting her ticket faster.
S4.feel: Anxious but slower, more a leak than a fire.
S4.quote: It's not a fire, it's a leak.
S4.fieldNote: The decade gives Priya time in her father's trade, which clearly matters to her emotionally. She still won't retrain but would steer her children away from being trapped in line work. Her public line stays deliberately low-key.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because we'd have nothing to fall back on and no time. What would help is if the company had to give people like me proper notice and a decent payout. And maybe some help with the mortgage for a while, so we don't lose the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what the job means. It's not just money for me. Every time I'm up a pole I think, Dad did this. If a robot does it, that's not just my job going, that's something of him going too.

headlineQuote: Every time I'm up a pole I think, Dad did this.
portrait: Priya Young is a 43-year-old junior lineworker on a rural crew in flat farm country, who came to her father's trade after twenty years of hairdressing. She and her partner Sam, a tyre-shop mechanic, have two kids, a mortgage and about two weeks of bills saved. She never uses AI, keeps her opinions low-key and blames no one in particular. She is calm when AI stalls, uneasy about gradual change, alarmed at both two and five years because she won't retrain, and only slightly less tense with ten years, falling back each time on cutting hair from her kitchen.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be nothing to fall back on and no time.
whatWouldHelp: Proper notice and a decent payout from the company, and some help with the mortgage for a while so they don't lose the house.
